summary: Describes two algorithms for IPv6, source address selection and destination address selection, giving default behavior for all implementations. They do not override choices by applications or upper layers. It was replaced by RFC 6724.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says how a host chooses between its own IPv6 addresses and how it orders the addresses a name resolves to. The rules are meant to be the same on every host, so that an administrator can predict what a machine will do.

questions: how does ipv6 choose a source address
what is the ipv6 default policy table
does ipv6 prefer ipv6 over ipv4
how are destination addresses sorted in ipv6
subtitle: The default rules a host uses to pick which of its own addresses to send from, and which address to try first.

tldr.problem: A node with IPv6 often has several addresses at once, and a name in DNS often resolves to several addresses, so something has to decide which one to use and in what order to try the rest.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two sets of pairwise comparison rules. The source address selection algorithm picks one source address for a given destination, and the destination address selection algorithm sorts a list of destination addresses, using a policy table that assigns a precedence and a label to each prefix.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3484 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 6724.

sections.title: Why Default Address Selection Is Needed
sections.content:
The IPv6 addressing architecture allows multiple unicast addresses to be assigned to interfaces. These addresses may have different reachability scopes, link-local, site-local or global, and may also be preferred or deprecated. Privacy considerations have introduced the concepts of public addresses and temporary addresses, the mobility architecture introduces home addresses and care-of addresses, and multi-homing situations result in more addresses per node. A node may have multiple interfaces, some of them tunnels or virtual interfaces, and a site may have multiple ISP attachments with a global prefix per ISP.

The end result is that IPv6 implementations will very often face multiple possible source and destination addresses when initiating communication. It is desirable to have default algorithms, common across all implementations, for selecting source and destination addresses, so that developers and administrators can reason about and predict the behavior of their systems.

Dual or hybrid stack implementations, which support both IPv6 and IPv4, will very often need to choose between the two when initiating communication. If a DNS name resolves to both a global IPv6 address and a global IPv4 address, and the node has a global IPv6 address and a 169.254/16 auto-configured IPv4 address, then IPv6 is the best choice. But if the node has only a link-local IPv6 address and a global IPv4 address, then IPv4 is the best choice. A simple policy of always preferring one protocol or the other produces poor behaviour, and the destination address selection algorithm solves this with a unified procedure for choosing among both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.

The selection rules specified in the document must not be construed to override an application or upper layer's explicit choice of a legal destination or source address.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can have many addresses, and a name can have many. This RFC fixes the order in which they are tried, the same way on every machine, so the result is predictable rather than arbitrary.

sections.title: The Policy Table and Address Properties
sections.content:
The policy table is a longest-matching-prefix lookup table, much like a routing table. Given an address A, a lookup produces two values: a precedence value, used for sorting destination addresses, and a classification or label, which allows policies that prefer a particular source address prefix for use with a destination address prefix. The algorithms prefer to use a source address S with a destination address D if Label(S) equals Label(D).

If an implementation is not configurable or has not been configured, it should operate according to the default policy table: ::1/128 has precedence 50 and label 0; ::/0 has precedence 40 and label 1; 2002::/16 has precedence 30 and label 2; ::/96 has precedence 20 and label 3; and ::ffff:0:0/96 has precedence 10 and label 4. One effect of the default policy table is to prefer native source addresses with native destination addresses, 6to4 source addresses with 6to4 destination addresses, and v4-compatible source addresses with v4-compatible destination addresses. Another effect is to prefer communication using IPv6 addresses to communication using IPv4 addresses, if matching source addresses are available.

The common prefix length of two addresses is the length of the longest prefix, looking at the most significant or leftmost bits, that they have in common; it ranges from 0 to 128. Because some address types have properties that are not directly comparable, mappings are defined. Multicast destination addresses have a 4-bit scope field, with values for interface-local, link-local, subnet-local, admin-local, site-local, organization-local and global scopes; unicast link-local is mapped to multicast link-local, unicast site-local to multicast site-local, and unicast global scope to multicast global scope.

IPv4 addresses are represented as IPv4-mapped addresses for the purpose of the algorithms. IPv4 auto-configuration addresses with the prefix 169.254/16 are assigned link-local scope; IPv4 private addresses with the prefixes 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16 are assigned site-local scope; IPv4 loopback addresses with the prefix 127/8 are assigned link-local scope, analogously to the treatment of the IPv6 loopback address; and other IPv4 addresses are assigned global scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy table is a routing-table-like lookup that gives every address a rank and a label. The label is what makes a source address and a destination address match up, and the default table is what makes IPv6 win over IPv4 when both are possible.

sections.title: Source Address Selection
sections.content:
The source address selection algorithm produces as output a single source address for use with a given destination address, and it applies only to IPv6 destination addresses. It is specified as a list of pair-wise comparison rules that, for a given destination address D, impose a greater-than ordering on the addresses in the candidate set. The address at the front of the list after the algorithm completes is the one selected. Conceptually a sort is being performed, but because the output is a single address an implementation need only identify the maximum value. Where a rule produces a tie, the remaining rules are applied in order to just those addresses that are tied, and if the eight rules fail to choose a single address, some unspecified tie-breaker is used.

The eight rules are: rule 1, prefer the same address, so if one candidate equals the destination it is preferred. Rule 2, prefer appropriate scope, so that an address whose scope is smaller than the destination's scope loses to one that is not. Rule 3, avoid deprecated addresses, preferring a preferred address over a deprecated one when the scopes are the same. Rule 4, prefer home addresses, so an address that is both a home address and a care-of address beats one that is only a home address or only a care-of address, and a home address beats a care-of address. Rule 5, prefer the outgoing interface, so a candidate assigned to the interface that will be used to send to the destination is preferred. Rule 6, prefer matching label, so a candidate whose label matches the destination's label is preferred. Rule 7, prefer public addresses over temporary ones. Rule 8, use the longest matching prefix, comparing the common prefix length of each candidate with the destination.

Rule 8 may be superseded if the implementation has other means of choosing among source addresses. Rule 2 must be implemented and given high priority, because it can affect interoperability. Implementations must provide a mechanism allowing an application to reverse the sense of the home-address preference, and a mechanism allowing an application to reverse the sense of the public-address preference; implementations for which privacy considerations outweigh application compatibility concerns may reverse the sense of rule 7 by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight rules are applied one after another to pairs of candidate addresses, and the first rule that separates two addresses decides between them. The most important is scope: an address that is too local to reach the destination loses.

sections.title: Destination Address Selection
sections.content:
The destination address selection algorithm takes a list of destination addresses and sorts them. It sorts IPv6 and IPv4 addresses together, and to find the attributes of an IPv4 address in the policy table the address should be represented as an IPv4-mapped address. The pair-wise comparison consists of ten rules, which should be applied in order; if a rule determines a result, the remaining rules are ignored, and subsequent rules act as tie-breakers.

Rule 1 avoids unusable destinations: if one address is known to be unreachable, or has no source address available, the other is preferred. Rule 2 prefers matching scope, where the scope of the destination matches the scope of the source that would be used for it. Rule 3 avoids deprecated source addresses. Rule 4 prefers home addresses. Rule 5 prefers a matching label between source and destination. Rule 6 prefers higher precedence. Rule 7 prefers native transport over an encapsulating transition mechanism such as IPv6 in IPv4. Rule 8 prefers smaller scope. Rule 9 uses longest matching prefix, comparing the common prefix length of each destination with its own source address. Rule 10 leaves the order unchanged.

Rules 9 and 10 may be superseded if the implementation has other means of sorting destination addresses. The RFC also notes that source address selection assumes routing, more precisely selecting an outgoing interface on a node with multiple interfaces, is done before source address selection, although implementations may use source address considerations as a tie-breaker when choosing among otherwise equivalent routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of candidate destinations is sorted with ten rules, the first being that an address which cannot work at all goes last. The last two rules are tie-breakers that keep the ordering stable.

sections.title: Implementation and Caching
sections.content:
The destination address selection algorithm needs information about potential source addresses. One possible strategy is for getaddrinfo() to call down to the network layer with a list of destination addresses, sort the list in the network layer with full current knowledge of available source addresses, and return the sorted list to getaddrinfo(). This is simple and gives the best results, but it introduces the overhead of another system call. One way to reduce that overhead is to cache the sorted address list in the resolver, so that subsequent calls for the same name do not need to resort the list.

Another strategy is to call down to the network layer to retrieve source address information and then sort the list of addresses directly in the context of getaddrinfo(). To reduce overhead, the source address information can be cached, amortizing the cost across multiple calls. In this approach the implementation may not know the outgoing interface for each destination, so it may use a looser definition of the candidate set during destination address ordering.

In any case, if an implementation uses cached and possibly stale information, or if the ordering of a cached list of destination addresses is possibly stale, then it should ensure that the destination address ordering returned to the application is no more than one second out of date. One strategy is to make a system call to check whether any routing table entries or source address assignments that might affect these algorithms have changed. Another is to use an invalidation counter that is incremented whenever any underlying state is changed, caching the current value with the derived state and comparing against it later to detect whether the derived state is potentially stale.
sections.plainLanguage: Sorting on every lookup is expensive, so implementations cache the result. The RFC asks that a cached order never be more than a second out of date.

sections.title: A Privacy Concern
sections.content: The document has no direct impact on Internet infrastructure security. It does note, however, that most source address selection algorithms, including the one specified here, expose a potential privacy concern: an unfriendly node can infer correlations among a target node's addresses by probing the target node with request packets that force the target host to choose its source address for the reply packets, perhaps because the request packets are sent to an anycast or multicast address, or because the upper-layer protocol chosen for the attack does not specify a particular source address for its reply packets. By using different addresses for itself, the unfriendly node can cause the target node to expose the target's own addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the choice of reply address is predictable, someone watching can work out which addresses a host holds by sending it traffic and watching what comes back.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT SOURCE ADDRESS RULES, IN ORDER

items.title: 1. Prefer same address
items.text: A candidate that is the destination itself wins.

items.title: 2. Prefer appropriate scope
items.text: An address too local for the destination loses. This rule must be implemented and has high priority.

items.title: 3. Avoid deprecated addresses
items.text: A preferred address beats a deprecated one.

items.title: 4. Prefer home addresses
items.text: A home address beats a care-of address.

items.title: 5. Prefer outgoing interface
items.text: An address on the interface that will be used wins.

items.title: 6. Prefer matching label
items.text: A source and destination with the same label pair up.

items.title: 7. Prefer public addresses
items.text: A public address beats a temporary one, unless the application asks otherwise.

items.title: 8. Longest matching prefix
items.text: The candidate sharing the most leading bits with the destination wins.
